questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Reason for a Discontinuity
questions.problem:
For what reason does the function $f(x)$ below have a discontinuity at $x=-1?$ 

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+x, & x<-1 \\ {x}^{2}+1, & x\ge -1\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2.$

- $f(-1)=(-1)^{2}+1=2,$ so $f(-1)$ exists. $✓$

- We calculate the one-sided limits and check if they coincide:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}({x}^{3}+x) \\  & =(-1)^{3}+(-1) \\  & =-2, \\ {lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =(-1)^{2}+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the one-sided limits exist but are not equal. $\,\,\times $ $\,\,\,$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=-1$ because ${lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x).$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Definition of Continuity to Evaluate a Limit
questions.problem: If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-1$ and ${lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{-}}f(x)=8,$ then what is the value of $\sqrt{f(-1)+1}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-1.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that ${lim}_{x\to (-1)}f(x)$ exists, and

$$
f(-1)={lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{-}}f(x)=8.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{f(-1)+1} & =\sqrt{8+1} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Definition of Continuity to Evaluate a Limit
questions.problem: If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=4$ and $f(4)=2,$ then what is ${lim}_{x\to 4}{({x}^{2}-6f(x))}^{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=4.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that ${lim}_{x\to 4}f(x)$ exists, and

$$
{lim}_{x\to 4}f(x)=f(4)=2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}{({x}^{2}-6f(x))}^{2} & ={({4}^{2}-6(2))}^{2} \\  & ={(16-12)}^{2} \\  & ={4}^{2} \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Reason for a Discontinuity
questions.problem:
For what reason does the function $f(x)$ given below have a discontinuity at $x=2?$

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}-2x+3, & x<2 \\ 2x-3, & x\ge 2\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2.$

- $f(2)=2(2)-3=1,$ so $f(2)$ exists. $✓$

- We calculate the one-sided limits and check if they coincide:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}(-2x+3) \\  & =-2(2)+3 \\  & =-1, \\ {lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}(2x-3) \\  & =2(2)-3 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the one-sided limits exist but are not equal. Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)$ does not exist. $\times $ $\,\,\,$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=2$ because ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)$ does not exist.

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Definition of Continuity to Evaluate a Limit
questions.problem:
If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=6$ and $f(6)=14,$ then

${lim}_{x\to {6}^{+}}\sqrt{f(x)+{x}^{2}-1}=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=6.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that ${lim}_{x\to 6}f(x)$ exists and

$$
{lim}_{x\to {6}^{+}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to 6}f(x)=f(6)=14.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {6}^{+}}\sqrt{f(x)+{x}^{2}-1} & =\sqrt{14+{6}^{2}-1} \\  & =\sqrt{49} \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$
